passage:
Nine-year-old Kishore slid his maths test under the sofa cushion. It was a 92, and the only mark that mattered to him was the missing eight. His father Yogesh never asked about the game they had played on Sunday or the lunch he had shared. He asked only, "What did you score?" and then, "Why not full marks?" Kishore began to hide any paper with a red cross, and learned to say, "It went well."

His mother Vasudha noticed him rubbing a hole into his notebook while erasing a tiny wrong figure. She felt proud of how hard he tried and worried that he was so afraid of mistakes. That evening she said, "Yesterday I burned the dal and forgot to buy tea. Everybody slips, and ordinary work is enough, you know." She did not tell him to lower his standards. Kishore looked at the notebook and laughed a little, a real laugh for the first time that week.

qa.q: What was the missing mark that mattered to Kishore on his 92 test?
qa.a: The missing eight mattered most to him.

qa.q: How do Yogesh's questions and Vasudha's evening talk show different parental responses to the same child?
qa.a: Yogesh responds only to marks, which makes Kishore feel loved for performance and hide his mistakes, while Vasudha, torn between pride and worry, shares her own mistakes and says everybody slips and ordinary work is enough, without shaming his high standards.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling when she saw the hole in Kishore's notebook?
qa.a: Vasudha felt proud of his effort and worried about his fear of mistakes, torn between the two.

qa.q: What could Yogesh ask instead of "What did you score?"
qa.a: He could ask about the day, the game and what Kishore enjoyed or learned, so that love does not seem to depend on marks.

grounding: Perfectionism in a household: a child hiding mistakes from a parent who responds only to marks, and another parent worried about tiny errors who shares her own mistakes.
